titulo: [$] Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers
resumo: Mike Lothian owns a docking station (or dock) that uses a DisplayLink chipset that had, at least in his opinion, subpar performance on Linux. He decided to try improving the Linux driver, with LLM assistance, but ran into one problem that he could not solve—so he asked for help, hoping that Synaptics's developers would lend a hand. Rather than help him in improving the driver, however, the Synaptics legal team responded with patent infringement claims, a demand that he cease unauthorized implementation of DisplayLink technology, and threats of expensive legal penalties. For now, it appears that Linux users of the company's docks will have to continue to live without feature parity with other platforms.

titulo: Kernel prepatch 7.4-rc2
resumo: Linus Torvalds has released the 7.4-rc2 prepatch and it will come as no surprise that it is a large one (" a big -rc2 to go with the largest ever -rc1 "). Much of the size was made up of some automated Coccinelle updates that were spread out all over the tree; once those are factored out, the rest looks fairly normal: When masking that noise out from the diffstat, the shape of it changes - not spread out over thousands of files any more. But it does not look unusual: a third is drivers (gpu, networking and sound account for most of it, but there's a bit of everything), another third is networking and bpf, and the final third is "the rest" (mostly filesystems, mm, arch updates). And yes, much of this was driven by various AI fixes. I think I'll stop repeating that, and we can just take it for granted. But this time around Alexei [Starovoitov] claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true.

With Zen 6, AMD’s next great gaming CPU could have it all
resumo: AMD’s best gaming CPUs have eight cores. Its next generation could pack twelve into the same kind of chiplet, making every single one of them faster. AMD’s Zen 6 architecture puts 12 full-performance cores and 48MB of shared L3 cache on a single chiplet, up from eight cores and 32MB with Zen 5. That’s a 50 percent jump in both, and AMD is rebuilding the cores themselves to squeeze more performance out of every clock cycle. The company revealed the finer details during a technical deep-dive into its next-generation Epyc “Venice” server processors. The next generation of Ryzen processors hasn’t been announced yet, but both families share the same underlying Zen 6 architecture. And for gamers, the implications go well beyond stuffing more cores onto a spec sheet, though that’s obviously fantastic. Twelve cores, one chiplet A core complex die (CCD) is a group of CPU cores sharing a pool of fast L3 cache, which keeps frequently used data close instead of forcing trips to slower system memory. Today’s 12-core Ryzen processors need two CCDs because Zen 5 fits only eight cores into each one. That works, but communicating between separate chiplets takes longer than communicating within one.

titulo: Windows 11 might be getting a central hub for app updates
resumo: Most Windows programs use their own systems to check for and install updates. However, this can result in an annoying number of reminders. It also carries the risk of missing important security updates. Windows Latest discovered that a new page for program updates has appeared under Settings > Apps in a preview version of Windows 11 26H2. The feature is based on the Windows Update Orchestration Platform (UOP), a technology Microsoft unveiled in 2025 that enables software developers to connect their existing update systems to Windows. The idea is that Windows will automatically check for available updates and schedule installations at suitable times. Among other things, the system can take into account whether the computer is in use, the battery level, and the network connection. Support is intended to cover traditional Windows programs installed outside the Microsoft Store, though this requires developers to connect their software to the system themselves. The new page is not yet fully functional, and it remains unclear when the feature will become available to all Windows 11 users.

titulo: Sharing a Windows PC? Why you should disable EFS before it’s too late
resumo: Windows’ Encrypted File System (EFS for short) is showing its age. Although it’s still very easy to use – just right-click on a file or folder and select Properties > Advanced > Encrypt contents to protect data – the risk of losing the decryption key is still pretty high. Unlike BitLocker, which encrypts an entire drive, EFS is designed to protect individual files and folders. This can be useful in some situations, but it also means that users may not always be aware of which data they have encrypted. That’s why most folks switched to alternatives like BitLocker, which comes with Windows, or VeraCrypt . The danger with using EFS is that you might encrypt important data, then delete your account and forget to backup the key beforehand. Unfortunately, there’s no way to decrypt data again after that. Especially on company PCs or computers used by multiple people. That’s why we recommend you disable the use of EFS.
